title: Learning to Persuade a Biased Receiver
claim: Probing from the conservative side costs little while overshooting loses everything, so safe exploration beats binary search with far lower regret.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid; two utility diagrams, then sample path and regret plot
description: A 2x2 grid of plots with captions (a) to (d). Panel (a) plots sender utility against the Bayesian posterior. A blue step function jumps from 0 to 1 at the threshold ν*=0.75. A red dashed line is the optimal scheme from (0,0) to (ν*,1), with a black dot marking the benchmark μ0/ν*=1/3 at μ0=0.25. Panel (b) uses the same axes. A teal dashed line marks a probe that overshoots to ν_R=0.89 and loses little (0.052). A red cross marks a probe that undershoots to ν_L=0.66 and loses a lot (0.333). Panel (c) shows a shaded uncertainty interval for the bias α shrinking over time t toward the true α*=0.7. Accepted probes are dots and rejected probes are red crosses. Panel (d) plots mean cumulative regret against horizon T. Binary search rises roughly linearly on a log-spaced axis. Safe exploration stays flat at about 5.
caption: Binary instance $B=(\prior,\qth)=(0.25,0.60)$ and true bias $\tbias=0.70$.
abstract: We study a repeated information design setting in which the receiver, who is also the decision-maker, updates beliefs in a systematically biased way. More specifically, a distorted posterior in our model can be written as a convex combination of the prior and the Bayesian posterior, governed by a fixed but unknown parameter. Over repeated interactions, the sender chooses persuasive signaling schemes, observes only the receiver's realized actions, and seeks to minimize regret relative to a full-information oracle that knows the receiver's biased updating rule. We propose a safe exploration algorithm for learning the receiver's bias while maintaining high persuasion value. The algorithm exploits the asymmetric cost of probing: conservative probes incur only local loss, whereas overly aggressive probes may lose the persuasive opportunity entirely. For general finite state and action spaces and arbitrary bounded utilities, our method achieves $O(\log\log T)$ regret. A matching $Î©(\log\log T)$ lower bound shows that this rate is optimal. We further discuss the influence on receiver welfare, as well as extensions to jointly unknown prior and bias, and contextual settings with time-varying priors and utilities.
